questions.solution:
Malaria: pathogen Plasmodium (P. vivax / P. falciparum), transmitted by the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito. Prevention — sleep under insecticide-treated bed nets; drain stagnant water / spray larvicides to destroy breeding sites.
Dengue: pathogen dengue virus (flavivirus, four serotypes), transmitted by the bite of infected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, which bite in daytime. Prevention — eliminate freshwater containers (tyres, pots) where Aedes breeds; wear long sleeves and use repellents during the day.
questions.question: Name the pathogen, vector and two preventive measures for EACH of malaria and dengue.

questions.solution: Antibodies are produced by plasma cells, the differentiated form of B-lymphocytes. Vaccination exposes the body to harmless antigen so memory B and T cells form — this is artificial active immunity: the person's own immune system makes the antibodies and remembers the pathogen.
questions.question: Which cells produce antibodies, and which type of immunity does vaccination provide?

questions.solution:
Innate immunity is present from birth, non-specific and immediate: e.g. skin/mucous barriers, phagocytosis by macrophages and neutrophils. Acquired immunity develops after exposure, is pathogen-specific and has memory: e.g. antibody production after infection (natural active), protection from vaccination (artificial active).
Interferons are signalling proteins released by virus-infected cells. They bind neighbouring cells and switch on antiviral defences (degrading viral RNA, blocking protein synthesis), slowing the infection while the specific response builds up — a key innate antiviral mechanism.
questions.question: Distinguish between innate and acquired immunity, giving two examples of each. What is the role of interferons?

questions.solution:
HIV (a retrovirus) binds CD4 receptors on helper T cells. Its RNA genome enters, and reverse transcriptase builds a DNA copy, which integrates into the host chromosome as a provirus. The cell then transcribes viral RNA, translates viral proteins, and new virions bud out, killing the CD4 cell. Falling helper-T counts collapse cell-mediated immunity.
Cure is hard because: (1) the provirus hides silently in long-lived memory T cells (latent reservoirs) untouched by drugs or immunity; (2) reverse transcriptase is error-prone, so HIV mutates extremely fast and escapes drugs and antibodies; (3) the virus directly destroys the immune cells needed to fight it. Antiretrovirals suppress replication but cannot remove integrated proviral DNA.
questions.question: Explain the life cycle of HIV inside a human host cell. Why is AIDS hard to cure even with antiretroviral drugs?
